newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan State Oil scrip seen undervalued.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan State Oil scrip seen undervalued.

text.p: Blue-chip Pakistan State Oil (PSO), which dominates the local oil products distribution market, is trading well below its real worth, James Capel Asia said on Monday.
"PSO is trading at a discount of 33 percent to our fair price valuation of 386 rupees ($9.60)," the brokerage house said in a report. "This blue-chip scrip is an essential buy."
PSO's 10-rupee shares closed at 306 rupees on Sunday, compared to a 12-month high of 367 and 12-month low of 196.

The state-run company commands 76 percent of Pakistan's oil products distribution market, worth an estimated 100 billion rupees a year. "A giant in the industry, PSO enjoys a 'quasi-monopoly' in the distribution market as its size acts as an effective barrier to entry," James Capel Asia said.

It said earnings were projected to grow 39 percent a year until 2000 as PSO exploited its size and market position to benefit from Pakistan's energy needs. Energy demand has been spurred by the power and transport sectors.
Demand for oil products is estimated to grow 12 percent a year until 2000, up from seven percent in the last five years.
PSO's agreements to supply furnace oil to 12 private power plants due to come on stream in the next two years are expected to increase sales volume by a compounded 17 percent a year.

Ammar Qureshi, financial analyst at James Capel, said PSO would benefit from an expected deal under which the government will increase the permitted profit margins of oil distribution companies in return for investments in infrastructure.

"There is an understanding between the government and the oil marketing companies that these margins will be doubled to four percent from the present two percent in the next four years, boosting PSO's profitability," Qureshi said.
He said higher profit margins could attract foreign oil ventures into a market that has stagnated for three decades.

"Competition is heating up for the PSO from Shell and Mobil. After the year 2000, the industry will be fairly liberalised and deregulated and then foreign oil giants like Mobil and British Petroleum might jump into the retail sector," he said.

The report said competition with Shell had intensified, especially in the deregulated lubricants market. Mobil was forming a joint venture with the Army Welfare Trust to market lubricants in a move likely to affect PSO's market share.
But Qureshi said the scrip was nevertheless a good buy and was expected to outperform the market in future.
PSO is 60 percent owned by the government, 26 percent directly and 34 percent indirectly through public sector financial institutions. Of the remainder, 17 percent is held by foreign investors.
